doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: The Ed Sullivan Show and the Jazz and People's Movement
summary: Rowe asks about the 1971 Ed Sullivan appearance; Griffin explains the Jazz and People's Movement and how the unrehearsed 'Kukumba' and Haitian Fight Song performance with Shepp and Mingus unfolded.

blocks.x: This morning I watched the now-classic or well known video of Rahsaan and the group on Ed Sullivan.
And there you are and I’m trying to think of a question here because it was quite an event. Do you remember how you felt afterwards?

Oh yeah. Because I could see the whole thing going up to that and afterwards and the whole thing. Okay that was the result of the Jazz and People’s Movement. We would go into these studios, Merv Griffin and all these different studios, The Tonight Show and everything, and just start playing New Orleans style music and interrupt their taping. So it went on and Mark — I forget the guy’s name — was part of it and he’s still around. But we would do this Jazz and People’s Movement. So we were trying to get jazz to be played on network television. And it happened for a short minute. I remember playing The Today Show with Frank Foster and I did the Ed Sullivan Show with Rahsaan, and various shows started to have jazz performances. It lasted a hot minute, a hot minute. And at that time Jimmy Owens was on the David Frost Show I think it was with Billy Taylor was the music director and Thad Jones was in the pit band of CBS. And I was in Thad Jones’s band at that time. All of that said, yes — so the show was — he had told Ed Sullivan, “We’re going to play ‘My Cherie Amour’” you know. And but when the show actually — it was a live show — when the camera came on to Rahsaan nobody knew exactly what he was going to do but we were thinking oh yeah, we didn’t even rehearse,

we were going to play “My Cherie Amour” and we had done that. That’s when he said “Kukumba” and then started with the whole thing. And everybody was just ready. And everything was on the spur of the moment and he introduced everybody later, Archie Shepp and Archie played, then Mingus, and the thing that Mingus and Rahsaan was doing was they played the dozens. And people don’t understand that, that’s when you’re talking back and you’re playing the dozens. Now I won’t even go any deeper than that because most people from the era know what playing the dozens is and that’s what they were doing on live television [scats]. And that was the language that we used and we played the dozens. And then he went into [scats] that’s the “Haitian Fight Song,” and we didn’t know. And everything I tell everybody, all of those riffs were made on the spot.
That was the question I had because I was watching you and at one point the camera was on the three of you in the horn section and I said, “I’ll bet they’re just like making that up and listening.”
